rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi regards as unreliable exegetical reports that at the Battle of the Ditch nearly all Muslims lacked courage, apart from one or two people.
rows.anchor: I regard unreliable the narratives found in our books of exegesis

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The siege and internal doubts put believers through a severe trial; such trials distinguish the good from evil elements.
rows.anchor: put the believers into a great trial and they were badly jolted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse expands the earlier depiction of suspicion toward God: hypocrites and Islam's hidden enemies called God's and the Messenger's promises fraud to demoralize Muslims.
rows.anchor: The Hypocrites and those who had malice against Islam in their hearts started to spread the propaganda

rows.speaker: some narratives
rows.claim: Some exegetical narratives report a sarcastic taunt that although Muhammad promised Persia's and Rome's treasures, Muslims could not even leave home to relieve themselves.
rows.anchor: Some narratives even record this sarcastic remark:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic word marad is used for two moral ailments, hypocrisy and jealousy, while context determines which shade applies when it occurs alone.
rows.anchor: used in the Qur’ān for two types of moral ailments: hypocrisy and jealousy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this construction, marad means jealousy and malice; elsewhere it can mean hypocrisy or jealousy, as illustrated by 33:32 and 47:29.
rows.anchor: it is used in its general meaning of hypocrisy and at some instances, it means jealousy and malice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites included weak-willed people and another faction that secretly harboured malice and enmity toward Islam.
rows.anchor: there were two types of people among the Hypocrites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about those with disease in their hearts distinguishes the secretly malicious faction from ordinary hypocrites; missing this distinction obscures the Qur'an's emphasis.
rows.anchor: To make this group distinct from the general category of Hypocrites the attribute

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Context identifies the group saying that Madinah cannot be endured as Bedouin hypocrites from the surrounding settlements.
rows.anchor: it is evident from concomitant indications that the reference is to the Bedouins among them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These suburban hard-line hypocrites professed Islam after Islam's political rise, pursued vested interests, avoided battles with excuses, and, when feigning participation, advanced the enemy's aims.
rows.anchor: Among those who had professed faith in the suburbs of Madīnah, there was a group of very die-hard Hypocrites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the Ditch, the hypocrites' efforts centred on frustrating and discouraging Muslims; these are the people discussed in the surrounding verses.
rows.anchor: all their efforts revolved around causing frustration and discouragement among them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their address 'O people of Yathrib' marks the speakers as villagers from outside Madinah rather than inhabitants of the city.
rows.anchor: Addressing the people of Madīnah by the words “O People of Yathrib” is a clear indication

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yathrib was Madinah's old name; the suburban hypocrites' continued use of it signalled that they viewed Muslim rule as temporary, a reading the Qur'an exposes through their address.
rows.anchor: Yathrib is the old name of Madīnah. After the Prophet’s migration, it came to be called Madīnah al-nabī and later just Madīnah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One faction used ostensibly sincere advice to urge Muslims to retreat, arguing that fighting the huge enemy force was futile and return home might win leniency.
rows.anchor: these Hypocrites advised the Muslims in a very sincere tone to back off

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word awrah means an insecure place.
rows.anchor: The word ٌةَر ۡوَع means “an insecure place.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second Bedouin hypocrite faction claimed its isolated homes were unsafe and sought the Prophet's permission to leave, seeking an escape route that would let the enemy achieve its aim.
rows.anchor: They presented this plea before the Prophet (sws) that since their houses are isolate and insecure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unsafe-homes excuse points to villagers around Madinah, not its residents; historical arrangements had already protected women and children.
rows.anchor: The details found in history regarding this battle show that prior arrangements had been made to protect women and children.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The excuse was baseless: their homes were not in danger, and they only wanted to flee the front.
rows.anchor: this excuse has no basis.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the pronoun could refer to Yathrib, contextual indications make its antecedent the houses; protecting them is a pretext for abandoning religion, which the hypocrites value least.
rows.anchor: the excuse of protecting the houses is merely an excuse; they actually want to run away from protecting and defending the cause of religion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here fitnah means a demand to apostatize or wage war against Muslims; Islahi endorses this interpretation, which Zamakhshari also adopted.
rows.anchor: I think that it is correct.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 4:91 describes the same hypocrite category as wanting to return to sedition when summoned to it.
rows.anchor: Verse 91 of Sūrah al-Nisā’ points to this category of the Hypocrites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith entails readiness to sacrifice life and wealth; these hypocrites had additionally promised the Prophet and Muslims they would fight if needed, despite their earlier battle absences and excuses.
rows.anchor: most of them had not participated in previous battles because of baseless excuses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A promise made with God brings heightened accountability; the warning connects to the rebuke in al-Saff against saying what one does not do.
rows.anchor: they will be held accountable for every promise made with God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fleeing a duty for fear of death or execution is foolish: life and death belong to God, from whom no one can escape and to whom everyone eventually returns.
rows.anchor: evading one’s obligation for fear of death or execution is not a wise policy at all.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The little remaining life of those who flee is stripped of blessing; fulfilling their duty would still have allowed them their lifespan and earned an eternal kingdom.
rows.anchor: the life of such escapers is totally stripped of blessings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic suppresses part of the clause before 'or His mercy'; Islahi supplies the sense 'or He intends mercy,' noting such ellipsis is common in Arabic and unlike Urdu style.
rows.anchor: In accordance with the linguistic principles of Arabic, a part of a sentence is suppressed before

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression min dūn can also mean 'against' or 'in opposition to.'
rows.anchor: The expression ِن ۡوُ د ۡنِّم also means “against” or “in opposition to.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse challenges anyone trying to evade God to identify who could save him if God intended harm.
rows.anchor: The verse means that if a person wants to evade God, he should state who

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone controls both harm and mercy, so evasion is pointless; the warning says no protector or helper besides Him can rescue them.
rows.anchor: Mercy and harm, both are in the hands of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that none can protect them besides God rejects both intercession, as idolaters expected from deities, and support through another person's power.
rows.anchor: A person can be helped through intercession as was the belief of the Idolaters with regard to their deities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An incomplete verb is suppressed before 'knows'; the wording is a severe threat that God has always known those obstructing the defence and will punish them.
rows.anchor: An incomplete verb is suppressed before ُمَل ۡعَی.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi identifies these people as hypocrites who avoided defending the city and stopped trusted fellow believers, inviting them to join them so no one would hold them accountable; the long defence line let them evade duty.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, this is a reference to the Hypocrites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A suppressed incomplete verb also precedes ya'tūna; al-ba's means defence, and these hypocrites participated only sparingly and for show, demoralizing defenders and summoning them to their barracks.
rows.anchor: Before the indefinite verb َن ۡوُتۡاَی too, an incomplete verb is suppressed, and the word َسۡاَبۡال means “defence.”
